name: Chien-Shiung Wu
tagline: The physicist who toppled a law of nature — and never got the Nobel for it
story:
In 1956, two theoretical physicists proposed that a fundamental symmetry of nature — the conservation of parity — might not hold true in weak nuclear interactions. The physics establishment scoffed. No one believed the elegant mirror-symmetry of the universe could be broken. But Chien-Shiung Wu, a Chinese-American experimental physicist at Columbia University, decided to find out for herself.

She designed one of the most exacting experiments in the history of physics. Working through the Christmas holiday at the National Bureau of Standards, Wu cooled cobalt-60 atoms to near absolute zero and watched which direction they emitted electrons. If parity held, the electrons would fly equally in both directions. They didn't. The universe, it turned out, had a handedness. Wu had shattered a law physicists had trusted for thirty years.

The two theorists who suggested the idea — Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang — received the 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics. Wu, who had done the brutal experimental work that proved them right, was passed over. She never spoke bitterly about it in public. She simply kept working, becoming one of the most respected experimentalists of the twentieth century, nicknamed 'the First Lady of Physics.'

Her grit wasn't just in the grueling experiment itself — it was in choosing rigor over recognition, proof over prestige, and showing up to the lab when everyone else had gone home for the holidays. The universe doesn't care about fairness. Chien-Shiung Wu didn't wait for it to.
